overview: Eotyrannus (meaning 'dawn tyrant') was a medium-sized carnivorous theropod from the Early Cretaceous of the Isle of Wight, England, living approximately 127–121 million years ago during the Hauterivian to Barremian stages. Estimated at around 5 metres in length, it is one of the earliest and most primitive known members of Tyrannosauroidea, the lineage that would eventually produce Tyrannosaurus rex. Unlike the later tyrannosaurids, Eotyrannus had proportionally long arms and a more gracile build, offering a window into the ancestral body plan of the tyrannosaurian lineage.

Eotyrannus lengi was described in 2001 by Hutt and colleagues from a partial skull and skeleton. Its discovery on the Isle of Wight (Wessex Formation) was significant because it filled a critical temporal gap in tyrannosauroid evolution, demonstrating that long-armed, moderately sized tyrannosauroids were present in Europe over 120 million years ago. This has informed debates about where the tyrannosauroid lineage originated and how it spread across Laurasia.

fossilSites.name: Wessex Formation
fossilSites.note: The only known locality; the Barremian-age Wessex Formation has produced a rich dinosaur fauna of theropods, iguanodontids, and sauropods.

articles.title: Discovery and Naming
articles.body: Eotyrannus lengi was described in 2001 by Steve Hutt and colleagues based on a partial skull, cervical vertebrae, forelimb, and hindlimb elements from the Wessex Formation of the Isle of Wight. The species is named after fossil collector Gavin Leng, who first recognised the significance of the material. Only one specimen is known, limiting the completeness of anatomical reconstructions.

articles.title: Early Tyrannosaur Anatomy
articles.body: In contrast to late-stage tyrannosaurids such as T. rex, Eotyrannus had proportionally longer forelimbs and a more lightly built skull, features consistent with the primitive tyrannosauroid body plan. This supports the hypothesis that the iconic short-armed, massive-skulled body form of tyrannosaurids evolved gradually from smaller, longer-armed ancestors during the Cretaceous.

articles.title: Biogeographical Significance
articles.body: The presence of an Early Cretaceous tyrannosauroid in England indicates that the tyrannosauroid lineage had a Laurasian distribution well before the Late Cretaceous diversification of tyrannosaurids. European islands of the Barremian period may have served as evolutionary refugia or dispersal routes for various theropod lineages moving between Asia and North America.

articles.title: Isle of Wight Fauna
articles.body: Eotyrannus shared the Wessex Formation ecosystem with the iguanodont Mantellisaurus, the sauropod Sauroposeidon, and other theropods. The formation is one of the richest Early Cretaceous dinosaur sites in the UK, and the Isle of Wight is sometimes called 'Dinosaur Island' in recognition of its palaeontological significance.

record.description: Eotyrannus lengi was an early tyrannosauroid from the Wessex Formation of the Isle of Wight. One associated partial skeleton preserves parts of the skull, vertebral column, girdles and limbs, documenting a lightly built, three-fingered relative of later tyrannosaurids.
facts: Only one incomplete individual is securely known.
The holotype was not fully grown, so adult dimensions are uncertain.
Serrated teeth support carnivory; prey and hunting style are not known.

review.ageReviewNote: The Wessex Formation occurrence is Barremian, with no direct date on the skeleton.
